title: Ibn Arabi
hook: the mystic born in Murcia, who traveled east to Damascus

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Rushd, the judge of Cordoba who argued that careful reasoning is a duty. Your line was: reason as a gift. Which question did you follow? Day nine hundred forty-one.

Yesterday's philosopher asks to meet a boy. The boy, in his own later telling, is barely grown, and people have been talking about him. Ibn Rushd rises to greet him and asks, more or less: is what you have found by inner opening the same as what we find by reasoning? The boy says yes. Ibn Rushd looks pleased. Then the boy says no. And between that yes and that no, the boy reports, the old philosopher went pale. The boy was Ibn Arabi, and the story is his own.

Ibn Arabi was born in Murcia, in al-Andalus, and never really stopped traveling. He went east, to Mecca, where he began a vast book called The Meccan Openings, and on through the cities of the Muslim world until he settled in Damascus, where he is buried. People called him al-Shaykh al-Akbar: the greatest master. What did he teach? Begin with a verse he and other Sufis return to. In Pickthall's translation: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." Ibn Arabi takes that line very seriously. In his reading, if God's face is wherever you turn, then the world is full of signs, and every moment can be a meeting. Elsewhere in the Qur'an, God says of each person, "We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." For Ibn Arabi, knowing that nearness is not a conclusion you reason your way to. It is something opened in you, the inner opening behind his no to Ibn Rushd. Reason goes far, in his view, but there is a kind of knowing it can't hand you. Now the honest part. Ibn Arabi's books are dense and daring, and Muslims have read them in sharply different ways. Among his Sufi readers he is treasured. Some scholars, Ibn Taymiyya among them, attacked parts of his teaching as error. Others defended him as a master misunderstood. That argument is still going. So the title on today's carry comes with two words attached on purpose. The greatest master, some say.
screen: `FROM MURCIA TO DAMASCUS.` · `WHEREVER YOU TURN, GOD'S FACE.` · `A KNOWING THAT IS OPENED, NOT PROVED.` · `REVERED BY SOME, ATTACKED BY OTHERS.` · then, large: `THE GREATEST MASTER, SOME SAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit with one mystery. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing you can't explain and don't need to solve right now. Why you're here at all. Where a person you lost has gone. Why one moment last week felt so full. Don't argue with it, and don't try to crack it. Just let it sit beside you, the way Ibn Arabi let his yes and his no sit side by side. If your thoughts start building an answer, set the answer down gently and come back to the question. If you pray, you can bring the mystery into your prayer. If you don't, just keep it company. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Arabi. The mystic from Murcia who traveled to Damascus, called the greatest master by those who love him, and argued over by those who don't. Today's word.
Your line: the greatest master, some say. Today, when a question has two true answers, let yourself say yes and no, and see what opens between them. Day nine hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Some Sufi orders study Ibn Arabi's works closely and visit his tomb in Damascus; other Muslim scholars have criticized parts of his teaching, and the debate over him continues.
